Debt avalanche or snowball? Change the repayment order while keeping the budget fixed

Four graphics compare starting balances, repayment paths, interest and extra-payment scenarios across three hypothetical debts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore repayment order with one fixed debt budget

Interactive planning lab

Fixed monthly debt budget$635
Months · highest rate first25
Months · smallest balance first25

Hypothetical three-debt schedules. Interest is charged monthly at nominal annual rate / 12 before month-end payments. Each active debt first receives its entered fixed base payment, capped at amount owed. The initial active base payments plus extra form one fixed household budget; released or unused base payments roll to the priority debt in the same month. Highest-rate order breaks ties by balance; smallest-balance order uses balances after base payments and breaks ties by rate, then debt letter. Zero starting debts receive no budget allocation. No fees, new borrowing, changing rates, contractual minimum-payment formula, arrears or credit-score effects are modeled. Not repaid means not cleared within 120 months; interest for an incomplete schedule is partial.

The central idea

A repayment comparison needs the same starting debts and total budget. Keep base payments in place, then show where released payments and extra cash go.

01

Separate the priority rule from the amount you can pay

The FCAC’s debt-repayment guide describes prioritizing either higher interest rates or smaller balances, while continuing required minimum payments on every debt. It also notes the importance of past-due accounts and the motivation a repayment approach may provide.

This comparison isolates the order of extra payments. Both strategies use identical debts, rates, illustrative base payments and a fixed total monthly budget. It does not compare an aggressive budget for one strategy with a smaller budget for the other.

The base-payment fields are modeling inputs, rather than calculations of contractual minimums. Actual obligations can follow different formulas or change over time. Reconcile those requirements before using an illustration to plan a payment.

02

Build one budget and keep released payments working

The default debts are CAD 5,000 at a 20% nominal annual rate, CAD 1,000 at 10%, and CAD 8,000 at 8%. Their base payments are CAD 125, CAD 50 and CAD 160 a month. Adding CAD 300 of extra monthly money produces one CAD 635 budget.

Each month, the model charges interest at the nominal annual rate divided by twelve. It then pays each active debt’s base amount, capped at the amount owed. The remaining budget goes to the selected priority debt. If that debt is cleared, unused money reaches the next debt in the same month.

When an account is repaid, its released base payment stays inside the CAD 635 total rather than disappearing from the plan. The final payment is capped at the total amount owed. The model does not assume any subsequent unused debt budget is invested elsewhere.

03

Read the difference inside the repayment paths

The highest-rate-first approach, often called an avalanche, directs remaining cash to debt A in the default example. The smallest-balance-first approach, often called a snowball, initially directs it to debt B. Both still make the other entered base payments.

After the first payment cycle, total debt is CAD 13,510 in both cases. The allocation differs: highest-rate-first leaves approximately CAD 4,658.33 on A and CAD 958.33 on B, while smallest-balance-first leaves CAD 4,958.33 on A and CAD 658.33 on B. Debt C has the same balance in both.

Later interest charges reflect where those balances remain. Under the defaults, both schedules clear during month twenty-five. The shared payoff month therefore hides a cost difference: interest totals about CAD 1,630.86 for highest-rate-first and CAD 1,712.87 for smallest-balance-first, a difference of approximately CAD 82.01.

04

Distinguish a completed schedule from a partial one

The charts stop after all debts are cleared or after 120 months. A “Not repaid” metric means the model did not clear the debt inside that limit. It does not mean repayment is mathematically impossible under every later schedule.

Interest for an incomplete path is only the amount charged within those 120 months. It must not be read as a full-life repayment cost. The matrix reports NR instead of a full-cost figure for such a case. A rising balance indicates that the entered payments do not cover modeled interest.

Balances are hypothetical and no credit limit, late fee, new purchase, rate change, promotional offer or lender intervention is modeled. The exercise cannot determine the effect of missed payments or predict a credit score.

05

Compare payment capacity alongside the ordering choice

The matrix changes debt A’s rate and the extra monthly amount while retaining the other selected inputs. Every cell uses the highest-rate-first rule and the same base-payment convention. It shows how the cost changes when the funding available to that rule changes.

The smallest-balance rule is based on current balances after the month’s base payments. Rate and debt letter resolve ties. The highest-rate rule resolves ties by balance and then letter. These conventions keep an otherwise ambiguous comparison reproducible.

A practical plan also needs a payment amount the household can maintain, funds for essential expenses and a review of actual account terms. Use the graphics to understand the cost of an ordering choice while keeping the budget, minimum obligations and ability to follow the schedule explicit.
